en: The forty children wept and screamed;
The children cried out in pain.
Manas stood, telling the Kalmyks,
“Stop! Stop!”
His cries of “Stop!” did no good;
The Black Kalmyks would not relent.
As Manas kept saying “Stop,”
The frenzied boys rushed at him.
Seven cudgel blows and four punches
Struck Manas.
When those cudgels struck him,
Without looking from side to side,
Your warrior unleashed havoc.
Without sparing his slender life,
Without looking all around,
Without sparing his life at all,
His face like oiled wheat,
His eyes like twilight mist,
His eyes blazed fiercely like fire;
The thirst for blood truly seized him.
His broad front teeth, like a gate,
Teeth unlike those of other people,
Bared themselves white.
When the forty boys lay beaten,
That fellow touched by Khizir
Now began an astonishing fight:
“Black Kalmyks and Manchu people,
Let me slaughter your whole people!
Your eighty have gone mad;
Let me rest only when I have slain them!
The children of the forty households—
You Black Kalmyks with your topknots!
You would not leave peaceful people alone;
Your cruel weight has fallen on them,
As though they had seized your fine horse,
As though they had started the trouble.
Who could bear this suffering?
If they press me, I will finish them.
These Kalmyks have grown overbearing;
Let me have a brawl with them!”
So spoke the warrior Manas,
Roaring in his fury,
Raising the battle cry, “Kyrgyz!”
Just watch that extraordinary boy:
A black foalskin coat on his back,
A black cudgel in his hand.
Swinging the cudgel in his grip,
He rushed upon the boys;
He passed among them as though at play,
And twelve boys died at once.
The eighty boys scattered in a panic,
Scattered and broke apart,
Chattering in Kalmyk,
Babbling in Chinese.
So many boys were thrown into panic,
Crowding together in mortal fear;
So many boys fled.
Fearing Manas, those children
Tumbled and fell;
In their terror the children's
Cries reached God.
Your Manas, in his fury,
Now spread utter havoc.
Twelve of the Kalmyk children
Now lay sprawled and dead.
As the children fled,
Manas raged without stopping;
The forty Kyrgyz boys
Gathered to stand beside him.
Of the eighty Kalmyk boys,
He crushed each one he met,
Heaped disgrace upon them like sheep.
Whoever exchanged blows with him,
Manas tore out his throat.
As he was about to finish them all,
Pursuing the boys,
About to tear all their coats,
About to swallow their blood if he caught them,
About to wreak a terrible slaughter,
Those Kalmyk boys,
Scattering every one,
As he drove them toward their village,
Scattering every one,
As he was about to finish them all,
Leaving none he caught unharmed,
Punching them sprawling as he went,
As the Kalmyks were about to learn,
As grave turmoil was about to arise,
His father, rich Jakyp,
Was surveying the grazing grounds.
Puffed up upon his gray stallion,
Ill-disposed rich Jakyp
Happened upon them.
Driving the forty boys back,
He seized Manas:
“Ah, my son, you have ruined me!” he said,
And poured forth sorrowful lament.
“I brought my herds here and raised them;
My Altay was a fine land.
Its people were good and generous;
My Kalmyks were a fine people.
If you go on like this, my son,
You will dig my pit;
You will boil, my little foal,
My misery from far away.
You will drain my strength;
Unless you cease this wildness,
You will have my herds plundered.
Your wildness knows no measure;
To meet them and strike with clubs,
The sea of Kyrgyz is not here.
My son, we wandered as exiles to Altay;
Your wildness reaches far.
Instead of behaving, you piss
Into my churn filled with kumys!
Wretched son, you will bring me
To utter ruin!
Unless you cease this wildness,
It will stir turmoil in my sleep.
Tomorrow will they not raid
My horses at pasture?
There is no forest to shelter in,
No Ogoy to seek refuge with.
Will the Kalmyks not do violence,
Unless you cease this wildness,
To the wealth I have gathered?
At last you will bring me,
Going on like this, to ruin.
Will they not draw a line through us all,
Unless you cease this wildness?
The Black Kalmyks, the many Manchus,
Will they not put me through wonders?
You will scatter, wretched son,
My gathered san of cattle.
You will have shed, wretched son,
My blood at these Kalmyks' hands.
Stop! You will cut off my life.
Unless you cease these doings,
You will set disaster going!”
Shouting at all the boys,
Jakyp drove them back and stopped them.
Having stopped them all,
He stirred up the past:
“Asking God for a child,
Truly a calamity
Is what I received!
You have not yet reached nine;
Why have you brought so much hell?
You will dig my pit.
If the Black Kalmyks rage,
They will bind my hands and take me.
Will they not show before my eyes
Wonders no person would devise?
‘Your son slaughtered children,’ they will say;
Will the Kalmyks not disgrace me?
My son, because of you,
The Kyrgyz living here,
Will they not slaughter them all?
The reason they would slaughter us:
The Black Kalmyks bear a grudge.
‘Manas will arise from the Burut’:
These infidels have from the beginning
Harbored that suspicion.
My son, your conduct,
The mischief you are doing,
Has been reported to their diviner.
Your name Manas has become known,
And in the seething infidels'
Register it is entered.
My son, are you starting a disaster?
You will bring down on my head
Wonders no mortal should see.
You will have measures taken against us.
The Creator has indeed granted
A wild child like you!
You will drain my strength,
You will have my herds plundered,
You will have the Chinese slaughter me,
Make a massacre of my life.
When your ancestors died,
When the countless possessions they left
Were divided by the Black Kalmyks,
Karakan's eight sons,
Every one of them scattered,
Were divided to every quarter.
One of us went to Iren;
We fell down thus,
Beyond what ears have heard or eyes have seen,
Into a pitiless depth.
For those who understand, we saw the Night of Power;
We came to Altay and made our living.
You killed children and raised a quarrel;
You will have my blood shed,
You will have my livestock slaughtered!”
Rich Jakyp spoke these words:
“Ah, my wild son!” he said.
Before an eye could blink,
Before another word was said,
My elder Baltay, bringer of good fortune,
Whose speech rang openly,
Among the forty households,
Your elder, old Baltay,
Akbaltay spoke these words:
“Your father's grave, hey, Jakyp!
Stop this scolding, Jakyp!
Go into the earth with your horses!
This son of yours named Manas,
He is our blessing, he our strength.
Beyond the Kalmyks, upon how many
Will this lion bring slaughter!
Let a boy be spirited!
Rather than be a son who tends herds,
Better he did not exist!
Your hands tied behind your back,
Driven here as captives,
We died on that day!
Thus, with much left unregretted,
If this son of yours grows,
He will bring great strife to Beijing.
My poor heart cannot gaze its fill.
If your son lives and grows,
He will bring great turmoil to the kakan!
He will gather your wandering caravans from the steppe;
My Manas will avenge
My long-distant wrongs.
If this Manas grows mighty,
If his fame resounds among the people,
If the way he faces is straight,
If the giants he spears and slaughters
Number exactly one hundred in renown,
Your spirits rose and you lived at ease.
When you had no child, rich Jakyp,
You kept a san of cattle and grew rich.
Can one put trust in herds?
Can your herds become a child?
You have seen your strength, Jakyp;
May the enemy seize your herds!
I hear what you amount to.
You begged God, hey, Jakyp,
For the only child He let you see.
Jakyp of great ancestral spirit and name,
Saying ‘My son will scatter the herds,’
You have now become a beast!
Understand what I say now.
You are foolish Jakyp;
Go into the earth with your herds.
Where is your ridge, where your mountain pass?
You fret over your herds;
Where are the Kyrgyz people blessed by Kydyr?
Saying ‘My son turned out wild,’
You have become disheveled.
Your heart smokes with grief,
As though an evil spirit had struck you;
You have taken pity on your herds.
Understand what I say now.
Do not grieve, rich Jakyp;
